title: Formation of Earth
summary: About 4.54 billion years ago, give or take roughly one percent, dust, rock and planetary embryos orbiting the young Sun collided and merged into the Earth; a last giant impact probably made the Moon.
card: Earth was assembled over tens of millions of years from planetesimals and Moon- to Mars-sized embryos left over from the Sun's birth. Lead isotopes in meteorites and ancient ores put the planet's age at 4.54 billion years, an answer first reached by Clair Patterson in the 1950s. Zircon grains from Western Australia show that a crust and probably liquid water existed by 4.4 billion years ago.
what:
Earth formed by accretion: in the disk of gas and dust around the newborn Sun, grains clumped into planetesimals tens of kilometres across, these grew into planetary embryos roughly the size of the Moon or Mars, and the embryos in the inner Solar System then collided with one another until a few rocky planets remained. Meteorite solids give the starting point of this sequence; the International Commission on Stratigraphy places the base of the informal Hadean Eon at 4,567 million years ago.

The age usually quoted for the Earth itself is 4.54 billion years, with an uncertainty of less than one percent according to the U.S. Geological Survey. It rests on lead isotopes: comparing the ratio of lead-207 to lead-206 in the oldest terrestrial lead ores with that in uranium-free minerals of iron meteorites such as Canyon Diablo. Clair Patterson of the California Institute of Technology calculated about 4.55 billion years in 1953 and published 4.55 ± 0.07 billion years in 1956; Tera's 1980 analysis of four ancient lead deposits gave the 4.54 figure now in common use. Earth's own oldest materials are younger, because plate tectonics has recycled the first crust: rocks of the Acasta Gneiss in Canada reach about 4.03 billion years, and a detrital zircon from the Jack Hills of Western Australia has been dated to 4,404 ± 8 million years.

The final large collision in Earth's growth is thought to have produced the Moon. This giant-impact hypothesis is the leading explanation, but its details are debated: whether the impactor, called Theia, was a single Mars-sized body or something else, how energetic the collision was, whether the Moon formed slowly from a debris disk or almost at once, and when it happened, with estimates from about 40 to 150 million years after the first meteorite solids. Scholars also note that it is not settled whether the 4.54 billion-year age records accretion itself, the separation of the core, or the material Earth was built from.

No continents existed during this interval, so the globe shows the whole planet without a map.

uncertainty.note: Start is the conventional age of Earth, 4.54 Ga with < 1% uncertainty (USGS; Tera 1980 via Dalrymple 2001); the minus bound reaches 4.567 Ga, the age of the first meteorite solids and base of the Hadean (ICS 2024/12), when accretion began. End is the Moon-forming impact, commonly given as about 4.5 Ga (NASA: ~60 Myr after the Solar System began); Hf-W estimates span 40-150 Myr after the first solids, i.e. about 4.527-4.417 Ga (Raymond 2024, citing Kleine and Walker 2017). Dalrymple (2001) notes it is unresolved whether 4.54 Ga dates accretion, core formation or Earth's source material.

how: The process ran in stages. Dust in the Sun's protoplanetary disk clumped into planetesimals about 10 to 100 km across, which grew by collisions (and possibly by sweeping up drifting pebbles) into planetary embryos of roughly 0.01 to 0.1 Earth masses. After the disk's gas dispersed, the rocky planets finished growing through a series of giant impacts between embryos. The heat of these impacts melted Earth, letting iron and iron-loving elements sink to form the core; the hafnium-182 to tungsten-182 decay system (half-life about 9 million years) records when this separation happened. The last giant impact, probably the Moon-forming one, ended the main growth phase. Afterwards, during so-called late accretion, smaller planetesimals added only about half a percent of Earth's mass. The planet's age is read from lead isotopes: uranium decays to lead at known rates, so the lead-207/lead-206 ratio in ancient terrestrial ores, compared with nearly uranium-free troilite in iron meteorites such as Canyon Diablo, fixes a common starting age for Earth and meteorites.
why_it_matters:
This is the opening event of everything else in the Atlas: every rock, ocean, organism and human story on the globe happened on the planet assembled here. Its outcome set conditions that still govern Earth. The giant impacts melted the planet and let iron sink into a core, separating it from the rocky mantle; the probable Moon-forming collision gave Earth a large satellite whose gravity is the main cause of ocean tides, and whose slow retreat from Earth is still lengthening the day. Within about 150 million years, zircons from Western Australia show, there was continental-type crust and probably liquid water, the setting in which life later began. If the final collisions had been different, Earth might have had no large Moon, a different mass or a different spin, and the history recorded on this globe would not have followed the same course.

The measurement matters too. Patterson’s 1956 meteorite-lead age settled a question on which early twentieth-century estimates had ranged from a few million to billions of years, and gave geology and biology a firm span of time within which evolution and plate tectonics had to fit. His later work to remove human-made lead from the environment, especially from petrol, grew out of the same laboratory methods. Today the 4.54 billion-year figure anchors the geologic time scale used by Earth scientists, and the Atlas’s own time axis begins at it.

perspectives.holder: Canonical giant-impact model (leading view; e.g. Canup and colleagues, summarised by Raymond 2024 and NASA)
perspectives.account: A Mars-mass embryo, Theia, struck an Earth that had about 90 percent of its present mass, and the Moon gathered from the debris disk. It explains the Moon's orbit, but predicts a Moon made mostly of impactor material, which conflicts with the near-identical oxygen isotopes of Earth and Moon unless Theia formed very close to Earth.

perspectives.holder: High-energy impact variants, including the synestia hypothesis
perspectives.account: A faster-spinning proto-Earth, an impact between two roughly equal embryos, or a collision so energetic that it made a doughnut of rock vapour (a synestia) would mix the two bodies thoroughly and so explain their matching compositions.
The Moon was built up from a series of smaller impacts rather than one giant collision.

perspectives.holder: Immediate-satellite model (Kegerreis et al. 2022; NASA and Durham University simulations)
perspectives.account: High-resolution simulations show a giant impact can place a Moon-sized satellite directly into orbit within hours, with outer layers about 60 percent proto-Earth material, easing the isotope problem.

NASA, from Apollo rock ages, gives roughly 60 million years after the Solar System began; hafnium-tungsten estimates span about 40 to 150 million years, and the chronometer depends on model assumptions.

The lead age is secure, but whether it marks the end of accretion, the separation of the core, or the age of the material Earth was made from is still uncertain; Dalrymple judged recent evidence to favour the last.
